title: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

relationships.phenotype: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract names homozygosity for a mild CTNS mutation as one cause of intermediate cystinosis. 'Intermediate' is a synonym for the late-onset juvenile/adolescent form.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: One mild mutation combined with one nephropathic mutation is compound heterozygosity in CTNS.

paragraphs.text: Late-onset cystinosis is a rarer form of cystinosis, a disorder caused by a defect in the transport of cystine across the lysosomal membrane. It is milder than infantile nephropathic cystinosis, and symptoms begin between 12 and 15 years of age (Attard et al., 1999).

paragraphs.text: Langman et al. (1985) reported late-onset cystinosis in a sibship. Thoene et al. (1999) found that intermediate cystinosis resulted from either compound heterozygosity for a mild mutation and a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation in the CTNS gene. paragraphs.text: In 6 patients with intermediate cystinosis, Thoene et al. (1999) identified mutations in the CTNS gene. Two of the mutations had not been reported before. The patients had either a mild mutation together with a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis (compound heterozygosity) or 2 copies of a predicted mild mutation (homozygosity). Transfecting cystinotic fibroblasts with normal CTNS cDNA, or with a cDNA carrying a mutation that causes intermediate cystinosis, partly corrected the cellular phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) screened the CTNS gene in patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, patients with late-onset cystinosis, and patients whose phenotype did not fit the classic definitions. They found 23 different CTNS mutations, 14 of which were novel. In 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis, the mutations affected regions of the predicted cystinosin protein that were not functionally important, which the authors suggested explained the milder phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) found that, of 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, 12 had 2 severely truncating CTNS mutations, consistent with loss of functional protein. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions predicted to disrupt the transmembrane domains and abolish protein function. In contrast, the mutations in 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin. Three patients had onset of cystinosis before 7 years of age but a milder course than the infantile nephropathic form. The authors suggested that the missense mutations in these patients allowed production of functional protein and might mark regions of cystinosin that are not functionally important.
